newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Cocoa seen heading for supply shortfall.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Cocoa seen heading for supply shortfall.

text.p: World cocoa supply is in "fair balance" and could be heading for a deficit in the long term if growers maintain self-restraint and robust consumption growth continues, a senior international cocoa official said.

The outgoing chairman of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) council, Jan van Sluisveld, in a recent interview with Reuters, also spoke against the reintroduction of market intervention to help defend prices.
"I would be surprised if people start talking about buffer stock mechanism in the future," said van Sluisveld, who has been involved with cocoa diplomacy since 1981.
"I don't think the importing countries will even consider the idea," he said.

Van Sluisveld, who was in London for last week's ICCO talks, is also stepping down as the head of the Dutch delegation to the ICCO following his move to another section of the Dutch agriculture ministry.
The ICCO, which comprises 36 key cocoa producer and consumer states, runs the five-year administrative pact that succeeded the previous economic agreements.
The previous pacts relied on costly buffer stock operations to help stabilise world prices.
Van Sluisveld said the present cocoa supply/demand picture indicated that cocoa was close to balance after seven years of straight surplus since 1984.
"Based on ICCO projections and if nothing peculiar happens, there will be a deficit and prices will go up," he said.
The ICCO agreed at the London talks to cut the world stocks-to-grind ratio, a barometer of prices, to 34 percent by the turn of the century from 67 percent in 1990/91 (October-September).
"We regard 34 percent as the normal level of working stocks," he said. "There will be no supply squeeze and prices will not skyrocket."
ICCO delegates have said that producers would need to cut world cocoa output, currently about 2.5 million tonnes, by 90,000 tonnes over the next three years to meet the target.
Critics say the ICCO's production plan could still be undermined by major non-member producers such as Indonesia and even by the members themselves.
Van Sluisveld said ICCO producer members, led by top grower Ivory Coast, should impose self-restraint to avoid over-production.

"If producers can cooperate with each other, they could help maintain the present situation of fair supply balance," he said. "This will ensure equitable prices for them and reasonable levels for consumers."
On cocoa demand, he noted eastern Europe, Japan, China and Brazil leading fast-growing chocolate consumption.
But he said prices at current levels of around $1,400 a tonne were at the lower end of the market range.
"The market decides on the value of cocoa but I was told that the industry could live with $2,000 a tonne," he said.
